column2: In the f-divergence, why does the definition insist that \(f(1) = 0\)?
column3: Because the argument of \(f\) is the density ratio \(P_x/P_\theta\). When the two densities are equal the ratio is 1 everywhere, and we want the divergence to be zero there. Any convex \(f\) with \(f(1)\neq 0\) would report a constant offset even for a perfect match.

column2: Why is \(D_f \ge 0\) for any admissible \(f\)?
column3: Jensen's inequality. \(f\) is convex and the ratio integrates to 1 against \(P_\theta\), so \(D_f = \mathbb{E}_{P_\theta}[f(u)] \ge f(\mathbb{E}_{P_\theta}[u]) = f(1) = 0\). Non-negativity is not an extra assumption; it falls out of convexity plus \(f(1)=0\).

column2: Which generator function \(f(u)\) turns \(D_f(P_x\|P_\theta)\) into the forward KL divergence?
column3: \(f(u) = u\log u\). Substituting gives \(\int P_x \log(P_x/P_\theta)\,dx = D_{KL}(P_x\|P_\theta)\).

column2: Which \(f\) gives the total variation distance?
column3: \(f(u) = \tfrac{1}{2}|u-1|\), giving \(\tfrac12\int|P_x - P_\theta|\,dx\).

column2: Is an f-divergence symmetric in its two arguments?
column3: Not in general. KL is the standard counter-example: \(D_{KL}(P_x\|P_\theta) \ne D_{KL}(P_\theta\|P_x)\). Jensen–Shannon and total variation happen to be symmetric members of the family.

column2: Forward KL \(D_{KL}(P_x\|P_\theta)\) takes its expectation under which distribution, and what does that make it punish most?
column3: Under the data \(P_x\). Its big terms are where the data has mass and the model has little, so it punishes the model for missing parts of the data.

column2: State precisely what we have and what we lack, when trying to minimise \(D_f\).
column3: We have samples from both distributions — the dataset for \(P_x\), generator outputs for \(P_\theta\). We lack the density functions themselves. So any usable objective must be expressible as an expectation over the two distributions, because expectations can be approximated by averages.

column2: Which theorem licenses replacing an integral with an average, and what exactly does it say?
column3: The law of large numbers. For iid \(x_i \sim P_x\), \(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} h(x_i) \to \mathbb{E}_{P_x}[h(x)]\) as \(n \to \infty\). It converts \(\int h(x) P_x(x) dx\) into a sum you can actually compute — which is why the entire next Part is spent rewriting \(D_f\) as a pair of expectations.

column2: In a GAN, where does a sample \(\hat{x} \sim P_\theta\) come from?
column3: Draw \(z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)\) and push it through the generator network: \(\hat{x} = g_\theta(z)\). We can sample \(P_\theta\) freely but never evaluate its density.

column2: What is the convex conjugate of \(f(u) = u\log u\)?
column3: \(f^*(t) = e^{t-1}\). Set the derivative of \(ut - u\log u\) to zero, giving \(u = e^{t-1}\), and substitute back.

column2: Write the variational lower bound on an f-divergence in terms of a critic \(T\).
column3: \(D_f(P_x\|P_\theta) \ge \sup_T\left[\mathbb{E}_{P_x}T(x) - \mathbb{E}_{P_\theta}f^*(T(x))\right]\).

column2: Why can an imperfect critic only under -estimate the divergence, never over-estimate it?
column3: Fenchel–Young: \(f(u) \ge tu - f^*(t)\) for every \(t\). A suboptimal critic is a suboptimal \(t\) at each point, so each pointwise term falls below its true value.

column2: Why does the bound become a supremum over functions rather than over a scalar?
column3: Because the inner problem is solved separately at each \(x\): the optimal \(t\) is a function of \(x\). If our function class is rich enough to contain that optimum we get equality; in general we get a lower bound, since we may be maximising over a restricted set \(T(x) \in \mathcal{T}\).

column2: In one sentence, what did the conjugate function buy us?
column3: It moved \(f\) off the density ratio. Instead of evaluating a convex function of \(P_x/P_\theta\) — impossible, no densities — we get an expectation of \(T(x)\) under real data minus an expectation of \(f^*(T(x))\) under generated data, both of which are sample averages.

column2: Maximise \(a\log D + b\log(1-D)\) over \(D \in (0,1)\). What is the maximiser?
column3: \(D = a/(a+b)\). This one-line calculation, done at every \(x\) with \(a = P_x(x)\), \(b = P_\theta(x)\), gives the optimal discriminator.

column2: What is the optimal GAN discriminator \(D^*(x)\) for a fixed generator?
column3: \(D^*(x) = P_x(x)/(P_x(x) + P_\theta(x))\) — the probability that \(x\) is real, which is a function of the density ratio.

column2: Against the optimal discriminator, which divergence is the generator minimising?
column3: Jensen–Shannon: \(J_{\text{GAN}}(\theta, D^*) = 2\,\mathrm{JS}(P_x\|P_\theta) - \log 4\).

column2: When \(P_\theta = P_x\), what does \(D^*\) output and what is the value of the game?
column3: \(D^* = \tfrac12\) everywhere, and \(J_{\text{GAN}} = -\log 4\). The discriminator can do no better than chance.

column2: How is the critic output \(T_w\) related to the discriminator probability \(D_w\) in the original GAN?
column3: \(T_w = \sigma_f(V_w) = \log D_w\), and \(f^*(T_w) = -\log(1 - D_w)\). Substituting into \(\mathbb{E}T - \mathbb{E}f^*(T)\) gives \(\mathbb{E}\log D + \mathbb{E}\log(1-D)\).

column2: Why does the critic need a special activation \(\sigma_f\) instead of being a plain network?
column3: Because \(f^*\) is only defined on a restricted domain. For the GAN choice that domain is \(\mathbb{R}^-\), so the critic must be forced to emit negative values. \(\sigma_f(v) = -\log(1+e^{-v})\) is exactly such a squashing, and composing it with a sigmoid is what turns the abstract bound into \(\log D + \log(1-D)\).

column2: The familiar GAN loss is usually presented as "classifier log-loss". What is it really?
column3: A variational lower bound on one particular f-divergence, with the f-divergence chosen so that \(f^*\) has domain \(\mathbb{R}^-\). The classifier interpretation is true and useful, but it is a reading of the formula, not the derivation.

column2: The objective is written \(\min_\theta \max_w\). Why can it not be written as a single minimisation?
column3: Because we are bounding a divergence from below and then tightening: the critic maximises the bound, the generator minimises it. The solution is a saddle point, and gradient descent on a saddle point is not guaranteed to converge the way it is for a minimum.

column2: Why does the generator's objective contain only one of the two terms?
column3: The term \(\mathbb{E}_{P_x}\log D_w(x)\) contains no \(\theta\), so its gradient with respect to \(\theta\) is exactly zero. The generator therefore sees only \(\mathbb{E}_{P_\theta}\log(1 - D_w(g_\theta(z)))\). This is also why the non-saturating variant of the loss exists — but that variant is not in these notes.

column2: In the two update rules, which parameter is held constant in each?
column3: Critic step: \(\theta\) is constant, \(w\) moves up the gradient of \(J_{\text{GAN}}\). Generator step: \(w\) is constant, \(\theta\) moves down. The generator's samples are computed with the fixed \(\theta\) during the critic's step, which is what makes the alternation well defined.

column2: What does the non-saturating generator loss maximise instead of minimising \(\log(1 - D(g_\theta(z)))\)?
column3: \(\log D(g_\theta(z))\): the log-probability that the critic calls the fake real. Same fixed point, much stronger gradient when the critic is winning.

column2: The critic gives a fake \(D = 0.01\). Per unit of critic logit, how strong is the generator gradient under the minimax loss versus the non-saturating loss?
column3: Minimax: slope \(\sigma(v) = 0.01\). Non-saturating: \(1 - \sigma(v) = 0.99\). The minimax gradient vanishes exactly when the generator is worst.

column2: What is mode collapse, and why does the GAN objective permit it?
column3: The generator emits one output or a few variations for every \(z\). The objective only asks it to fool the critic, and one reliably-fooling image does that without covering the data.

column2: In a DCGAN, what layer type grows the latent code into an image?
column3: Transpose (up-)convolutions, which upsample a small code such as \(z \in \mathbb{R}^{16}\) to a \(3 \times r \times c\) image tensor.

column2: In a conditional GAN, which network receives the condition \(y\)?
column3: Both. The generator computes \(g_\theta(z, y)\) and the discriminator scores the pair \(D_w(x, y)\).

column2: Why must a cGAN discriminator see the label as well as the image?
column3: Otherwise any realistic image fools it regardless of class, so the generator has no reason to obey \(y\). Judging the pair is what forces the image to match the label.

column2: Does "the classifier can no longer tell real from fake" imply \(P_x = P_\theta\)?
column3: No. Equal distributions make every classifier fail, but a particular classifier can fail on different distributions (e.g. a linear one against clusters it cannot separate). Hence the critic must keep adapting.

column2: Real data is a point mass at 0, the generator a point mass at \(\theta \neq 0\). What is their Jensen–Shannon divergence?
column3: \(\log 2\), for every \(\theta \neq 0\): the maximum, because the supports do not overlap. Its gradient in \(\theta\) is zero.

column2: Same two point masses. What is their Wasserstein distance?
column3: \(|\theta|\) — the mass must travel distance \(|\theta|\). It shrinks as the generator approaches, so it gives a useful gradient.

column2: Why, geometrically, do the supports of \(P_x\) and \(P_\theta\) usually fail to overlap?
column3: The manifold hypothesis: both live on thin low-dimensional surfaces inside \(\mathbb{R}^d\), and two such surfaces in general position almost never intersect.

column2: Explain why a perfect discriminator halts training.
column3: With disjoint supports the critic can be 100% accurate, so \(D_f(P_x \| P_\theta)\) no longer varies with \(\theta\). The generator's gradient is zero even though the generator is terrible. Training has saturated on a number that has stopped carrying information.

column2: What is the fix, stated as a requirement on the divergence?
column3: Use a softer metric that does not saturate when the supports fail to align — one that still reports a meaningful gradient even for disjoint distributions. That requirement is what leads to the Wasserstein metric.

column2: \(P_x\) puts mass \(\tfrac12\) on each of \(\{0, 1\}\); \(P_\theta\) puts \(\tfrac12\) on each of \(\{2, 3\}\). What is \(W_1\)?
column3: 2. Ship 0→2 and 1→3: each unit of mass travels 2, so the cheapest average work is 2.

column2: What is a transport plan, concretely?
column3: A joint distribution over pairs \((x, \hat{x})\) whose marginals are \(P_x\) and \(P_\theta\). As a table, entry \((i,j)\) says how much mass moves from real point \(x_i\) to fake point \(\hat{x}_j\). Row sums are \(P_x\), column sums are \(P_\theta\).

column2: What happens to the WGAN critic objective if the 1-Lipschitz constraint is dropped?
column3: It becomes unbounded: scaling any critic that separates the data by \(c\) multiplies the objective by \(c\), so the supremum is \(\infty\) and carries no information.

column2: State the 1-Lipschitz condition on the critic.
column3: \(|T_w(x_1) - T_w(x_2)| \le \|x_1 - x_2\|\) for all \(x_1, x_2\): the critic’s output may not change faster than its input.

column2: Name two crude ways to keep the WGAN critic Lipschitz after each gradient step.
column3: Clip every weight into \([-c, c]\) (the original paper), or renormalise the weights so \(\|w\|_2 = 1\) (the notes).

column2: Write the WGAN critic objective (Kantorovich–Rubinstein dual).
column3: \(\max_{\|T_w\|_L \le 1}\ \mathbb{E}_{P_x}T_w(x) - \mathbb{E}_{P_\theta}T_w(\hat{x})\). No sigmoid, no log — just a difference of means.

column2: In WGAN-GP, where is the gradient penalty evaluated, and what does it penalise?
column3: At random interpolates \(\tilde{x} = \epsilon x + (1-\epsilon)\hat{x}\) between real and fake samples; it penalises \((\|\nabla_{\tilde{x}}T_w\|_2 - 1)^2\).

column2: Why is a trained GAN generator not invertible by formula?
column3: \(g_\theta: Z \to X\) is a many-to-one neural map with no closed-form inverse, so recovering \(z\) from \(x\) needs a learned encoder or an optimisation.

column2: What extra loss term does latent-regression GAN inversion add?
column3: \(\alpha\,\mathbb{E}_{\hat{x}\sim P_\theta}\|z - E_\phi(\hat{x})\|_2^2\): the encoder must recover the \(z\) that generated each fake.

column2: In a BiGAN, what does the discriminator actually compare?
column3: Tuples, not samples. It sees \((x, E_\phi(x))\) from the real-plus-encoder side and \((g_\theta(z), z)\) from the generator side. The optimum is reached when \(P_{\hat{z}x} = P_{z\hat{x}}\) — the joint distribution of data with its code matches the joint of code with its generated image.

column2: In domain-adversarial training, what are the two objectives of the feature extractor \(\Phi\)?
column3: (a) Classification: features must predict source labels through \(h_\psi\). (b) Adversarial: features must make source and target indistinguishable to a domain discriminator.

column2: In domain-adversarial training, why does making the discriminator fail help the classifier?
column3: If the discriminator cannot tell source features from target features, then \(P_{f_s} = P_{f_t}\): the feature distribution is domain-invariant. A classifier trained on source features therefore sees inputs drawn from the same distribution at test time on the target domain.

column2: Why not compare generated and real images pixel by pixel?
column3: Per-pixel distance is dominated by trivial misalignments and says nothing about whether the images are plausible. FID instead compares statistics of deep features, where semantic content is represented and small spatial shifts cost little.

column2: What does the first FID term, \(\|\mu_{\text{true}} - \mu_{\text{gen}}\|_2^2\), measure?
column3: How far the centre of the generated features has drifted from the centre of the real ones — a shift in average content.

column2: What does the trace term of FID measure?
column3: Whether the covariances match: the spread and correlation structure of the features. Too little variety (mode collapse) shows up here.

column2: What does FID reduce to in one dimension?
Real features: mean 0, s.d. 1. Generated: mean 0.5, s.d. 0.5. What is the 1-D FID?
What assumption does FID make that you should keep in mind before quoting it?
column3: That the layer-\(l\) features of each dataset are Gaussian, and that one pretrained Inception network on ImageNet is an appropriate judge. Both are convenient fictions; FID numbers are comparable within one setup, not across different feature extractors or layer choices.

column2: Why does the Kantorovich–Rubinstein dual (a 1-Lipschitz critic) give \(W_1\) and not \(W_2\)?
column3: The duality with a Lipschitz critic is a theorem about the cost \(\|x - \hat{x}\|\), i.e. \(W_1\). FID uses \(W_2^2\) instead because it has a closed form for Gaussians.

column2: How is a multi-layer network’s Lipschitz constant bounded, and what does that imply for weight normalisation?
column3: By the product of each layer’s operator norm (with 1-Lipschitz activations). So normalisation must act per layer — spectral normalisation divides each by its largest singular value.

column2: Why is a GAN’s training loss a poor measure of sample quality?
column3: It is a lower bound whose gap depends on how good the critic currently is, and the critic keeps changing. A falling loss may mean a weaker critic, not a better generator.
